description:
The Gori Temple — *Gori jo Mandar*, the "temple of Gori" — is a marble *Śvetāmbara Jain* temple standing amid the desert near the village of Gori, between Islamkot and Nagarparkar in Tharparkar District, some fourteen miles north-west of the Viravah ruins. Built in 1375-1376 CE and dedicated to *Parshvanatha*, the twenty-third *Tirthankara* of the Jain faith, it is one of the most important surviving Jain monuments of the subcontinent's north-west. The temple, raised on a high stepped platform and built of marble, measures roughly 125 by 60 feet and is distinguished by its three *mandapas* (halls) and its remarkable array of some fifty-two domes, whose form blends Gujarati temple design with the regional architecture of the age. Its greatest treasure is its painting: the frescoes within the main dome — depicting princely processions, palanquins and coaches, riders, and elegantly robed figures in flowing Rajasthani dress — are reckoned to be the oldest surviving Jain frescoes in the northern regions of the subcontinent, a survival of extraordinary rarity. Long abandoned as a place of worship, the temple stands today as a monument of the once-flourishing Jain and Hindu culture of the Thar. It forms part of the group of Nagarparkar temples inscribed in 2016 on the UNESCO tentative list as the "Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape," and it remains a site of pilgrimage interest for Jains and Hindus and of growing concern for heritage conservation.

A heritage-preservation survey by the Endowment Fund Trust for the Heritage of Sindh records the temple's main structure as built of a Jodhpuri stone "much like marble," and notes that its last major repairs are recorded to have been carried out in 1715, attributing the damage the temple has suffered over the centuries to Sindhi troops, fire, and gunpowder rather than to the earthquake and British demolition reported elsewhere. Press coverage in 2016 has independently repeated the temple's dedication to Parshvanath and dated its construction only to "around the 16th century" — a looser dating than the 1375-1376 CE given above, which this entry has not reconciled with the more specific figure. The site was already known to colonial-era archaeology: Henry Cousens' 1929 survey of Sindh's antiquities indexes "Gori" among its subjects, though its descriptive passage on the temple itself was not retrieved in this research pass.

## Bibliography

- "Gori Temple," Heritage of Sindh (Endowment Fund Trust for Preservation of the Heritage of Sindh), https://heritage.eftsindh.com/districts/tharparkar/gori-temple.php.
- Ema Anis, "Secrets of Thar: A Jain temple, a mosque and a 'magical' well," *Dawn*, 19 February 2016.
- Henry Cousens, *The Antiquities of Sind, with Historical Outline* (Calcutta: Government of India Central Publication Branch, 1929).
qa_note: This addition's verdict is PARTIAL: only two independent sources were verified in this research pass, and this entry's own pre-existing founding date of 1375-1376 CE is not among the facts corroborated here. The research pass surfaced two further unresolved conflicts. On the founding date: no source fetched in this pass supports 1375-1376 CE specifically; the Endowment Fund Trust for the Heritage of Sindh gives no date at all, and Dawn (2016) gives only "around the 16th century"; Wikipedia's own article on the temple (used only as an uncited pointer, not verified here) separately carries a legend of construction in 300 CE and itself flags the 1375-1376 CE figure as needing a citation. On the cause of historical damage: the Endowment Fund Trust attributes it to "Sindhi troops," fire, and gunpowder, with repairs recorded in 1715, while Dawn (2016) instead attributes wall destruction to an earthquake and to demolition by the British. Neither conflict is resolved here.
